Optimal Stochastic Bilevel Optimization with First-Order Oracles

Linxuan Pan    Junchi Yang Affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen Email: linxuanpan@link.cuhk.edu.cn yangjunchi@cuhk.edu.cn
Abstract

We study nonconvex–strongly-convex bilevel optimization under a stochastic first-order oracle. We introduce MRT-FD, a single-loop first-order method that simultaneously tracks the upper-level variable, the lower-level solution, and the auxiliary response arising from implicit differentiation of the hyperobjective. MRT-FD performs one update of each variable per iteration and approximates the second-order derivative actions using order-pp finite differences. For any fixed finite smoothness order p≥1p\geq 1 in the lower-level variable, MRT-FD finds an ε\varepsilon-stationary point using 𝒪⁡(ε−4−2/p)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4-2/p}) stochastic gradient queries. We also prove a matching Ω⁡(ε−4−2/p)\Omega(\varepsilon^{-4-2/p}) oracle lower bound. The lower-bound construction starts from a hard nonconvex minimization chain with a stronger stochastic oracle, and lifts it to a bilevel problem through a sinusoidal coupling with a scalar lower-level variable. Consequently, the dependence on ε\varepsilon is optimal for every fixed finite pp, closing the upper–lower complexity gap in this stochastic first-order oracle setting.

1 Introduction

Bilevel optimization models problems in which the performance of one decision depends on the solution of another optimization problem. We study the stochastic nonconvex–strongly-convex (NC–SC) setting

minx∈ℝdx⁡Φ⁡(x):=f⁡(x,y⋆​(x)),y⋆​(x):=arg​miny∈ℝdy⁡g​(x,y),\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}}\ \Phi(x):=f(x,y^{\star}(x)),\qquad y^{\star}(x):=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}}g(x,y), (1)

where g⁡(x,⋅)g(x,\cdot) is strongly convex and the hyperobjective Φ\Phi may be nonconvex. This formulation captures applications including hyperparameter optimization (Franceschi et al., 2018), data reweighting (Pan et al., 2025), and meta-learning (Finn et al., 2017).

Under standard smoothness conditions, Φ\Phi is a smooth nonconvex function. Writing H⁡(x,y):=∇y​y2​g​(x,y)H(x,y):=\nabla^{2}_{yy}g(x,y) and J⁡(x,y):=∇x​y2​g​(x,y)J(x,y):=\nabla^{2}_{xy}g(x,y), implicit differentiation gives

∇Φ​(x)=∇xf​(x,y⋆​(x))−J⁡(x,y⋆​(x))​H​(x,y⋆​(x))−1​∇yf​(x,y⋆​(x)).\nabla\Phi(x)=\nabla_{x}f(x,y^{\star}(x))-J(x,y^{\star}(x))H(x,y^{\star}(x))^{-1}\nabla_{y}f(x,y^{\star}(x)). (2)

The hypergradient therefore involves second-order derivatives of gg, motivating methods based on Hessian- and Jacobian-vector products (Ghadimi and Wang, 2018; Ji et al., 2021). When such second-order stochastic derivative information is available, an 𝒪⁡(ϵ−4)\mathcal{O}({\epsilon}^{-4}) oracle complexity is achievable for finding an ϵ{\epsilon}-stationary point, matching the ϵ{\epsilon} dependence inherited from the lower bound for stochastic nonconvex optimization (Arjevani et al., 2023).

For large-scale problems, however, even Hessian-vector products may be expensive or unavailable, motivating methods that use only first-order queries. This restriction substantially changes the known complexity. Under standard smoothness assumptions, the best first-order methods achieve an 𝒪⁡(ϵ−6)\mathcal{O}({\epsilon}^{-6}) stochastic oracle complexity (Chen et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2026b). Recently, Chen et al. (2026b) show that additional ppth-order smoothness with respect to the lower variable yy can improve the upper bound to 𝒪~​(ϵ−4−2/p)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}({\epsilon}^{-4-2/p}). As pp increases, this rate interpolates between the ϵ−6{\epsilon}^{-6} complexity under base smoothness and the ϵ−4{\epsilon}^{-4} benchmark available with second-order information.

This improvement raises a fundamental question. Existing lower bounds do not characterize how the complexity of a first-order stochastic bilevel oracle depends on the available smoothness order pp. It remains unclear whether the exponent 4+2/p4+2/p reflects an intrinsic information-theoretic barrier.

What is the optimal complexity of stochastic NC–SC bilevel optimization under a first-order oracle, and how does higher-order smoothness in the lower variable change this complexity?

We answer the question above by sharpening both the upper and lower complexity bounds.

A single-loop first-order algorithm.

We develop Moving-Target Tracking with Finite Differences (MRT-FD), a single-loop method that requires order-pp smoothness only for gg with respect to the lower variable yy, for any p≥1p\geq 1. We introduce the auxiliary vector z⋆​(x)z^{\star}(x) as the unique solution of

H⁡(x,y⋆​(x))​z⋆​(x)=∇yf​(x,y⋆​(x)).H(x,y^{\star}(x))z^{\star}(x)=\nabla_{y}f(x,y^{\star}(x)).

MRT-FD maintains yky_{k} and zkz_{k} to track the moving targets y⋆​(xk)y^{\star}(x_{k}) and z⋆​(xk)z^{\star}(x_{k}) while simultaneously updating the outer variable xkx_{k}. It uses order-pp finite differences to reconstruct the required second-order derivative actions from first-order queries, while projection keeps zkz_{k} bounded and controls the resulting finite-difference errors. Our analysis couples objective descent with the tracking errors ‖yk−y⋆​(xk)‖2\|y_{k}-y^{\star}(x_{k})\|^{2} and ‖zk−z⋆​(xk)‖2\|z_{k}-z^{\star}(x_{k})\|^{2} through a moving-target Lyapunov function that jointly controls target motion, finite-difference bias, and stochastic variance. For fixed pp, it achieves 𝒪⁡(ϵ−4−2/p)\mathcal{O}({\epsilon}^{-4-2/p}) complexity, matching the ϵ{\epsilon} dependence of Chen et al. (2026b) while removing the logarithmic factor.

Lower bound for finite smoothness order pp.

We establish a matching lower bound under the same assumptions and oracle model. The construction embeds a hard nonconvex chain into a bilevel problem with a scalar lower-level variable through a sinusoidal coupling. Setting a coupling scale to δ=ϵ1/p\delta={\epsilon}^{1/p} preserves the required order-pp smoothness while keeping the resulting hyperobjective close to the hard chain. We then construct a stochastic oracle in which informative observations occur only through a rare Bernoulli event with probability ϖ=Θ⁡(δ2​ϵ2)\varpi=\Theta(\delta^{2}{\epsilon}^{2}). A random-rotation argument limits progress along the hidden chain for arbitrary adaptive randomized algorithms. Combining a chain of length T=Θ⁡(ϵ−2)T=\Theta({\epsilon}^{-2}) with the reveal probability gives the lower bound of Ω⁡(T/ϖ)=Ω⁡(ϵ−4−2/p)\Omega(T/\varpi)=\Omega({\epsilon}^{-4-2/p}).

1.1 Related Work

Bilevel optimization with second-order information.

Classical bilevel methods compute the hypergradient using second-order information. Iterative differentiation (ITD) differentiates through a finite lower-level trajectory (Domke, 2012; Shaban et al., 2019; Bolte et al., 2021), whereas approximate implicit differentiation (AID) approximates the inverse-Hessian–gradient product through linear-system or Neumann-type solvers (Pedregosa, 2016; Ghadimi and Wang, 2018; Grazzi et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2021).

In stochastic NC–SC bilevel optimization, methods such as stocBiO (Ji et al., 2021) and SUSTAIN (Khanduri et al., 2021) construct hypergradient estimators using Hessian- and Jacobian-vector products. SOBA/SABA (Dagréou et al., 2022) and MA-SOBA (Chen et al., 2024b) instead track the associated linear-system solution jointly with the lower and upper-level variables. These methods are structurally related to MRT-FD through linear-system tracking, but require second-order derivative information.

First-order bilevel optimization.

Fully first-order methods often rely on value-function or penalty reformulations, including BOME (Liu et al., 2022), penalty-based bilevel gradient methods (Shen and Chen, 2023), and F2SA (Kwon et al., 2023). Subsequent work improves the first-order oracle complexity through refined penalty and two-timescale schemes (Kwon et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025). More recently, SGHA (Gu et al., 2026b) develops a single-loop method based on a constrained reformulation of lower-level stationarity and finite-difference approximations, achieving 𝒪⁡(ϵ−6)\mathcal{O}({\epsilon}^{-6}) complexity, but requires additional assumptions in the boundedness.

FdeHBO (Yang et al., 2023) is the closest structural comparison to MRT-FD: it tracks the auxiliary linear-system solution using projection and finite-difference Hessian-vector approximations. Its guarantees, however, rely on stronger stochastic assumptions, including stochastic smoothness and unbiased stochastic Hessian estimates with bounded variance. FdeHBO uses variance reduction and reuses the same sample across multiple query points, whereas MRT-FD uses fresh independent samples and order-pp finite differences. Their analyses track different auxiliary errors: FdeHBO uses the current lower-level linear-system solution, while we directly control ‖zk−z⋆​(xk)‖2\|z_{k}-z^{\star}(x_{k})\|^{2}.

Chen et al. (2026b) show that ppth-order smoothness in the lower variable can improve the complexity from 𝒪~​(ϵ−6)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}({\epsilon}^{-6}) to 𝒪~​(ϵ−4−2/p)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}({\epsilon}^{-4-2/p}). Their F2SA-pp method uses high-order finite differences within a penalty formulation over perturbed lower-level problems, and assumes higher-order smoothness of both ff and gg in yy. In contrast, our additional order-pp smoothness condition is imposed only on gg.

Lower bounds.

Ji and Liang (2023) established lower complexity bounds for convex–strongly-convex and strongly-convex–strongly-convex bilevel problems, while Dagréou et al. (2024) derived matching lower bounds for finite-sum bilevel empirical-risk minimization. Beyond the strongly-convex lower-level setting, Chen et al. (2024a) showed hardness results for finding stationary points of the hyperobjective when the lower-level problem is only convex. For stochastic NC–SC bilevel optimization, Kwon et al. (2024) establish lower bounds under a y⋆y^{\star}-aware oracle, where unbiased bounded-variance stochastic gradients are guaranteed only locally around y⋆​(x)y^{\star}(x), making their setting not directly comparable to ours. More recently, Chen et al. (2026a) prove an Ω⁡(κ4.5​ϵ−4)\Omega(\kappa^{4.5}{\epsilon}^{-4}) lower bound for NC–SC bilevel optimization, where κ\kappa denotes the condition number, while concurrent work by Gu et al. (2026a) establishes an Ω⁡(κ8​ϵ−6)\Omega(\kappa^{8}{\epsilon}^{-6}) lower bound. Our result complements these works by characterizing the effect of higher-order smoothness in the lower variable: for a fixed pp, we prove a Ω⁡(ϵ−4−2/p)\Omega({\epsilon}^{-4-2/p}) lower bound.

2 Problem Setting and Oracle Model

We consider the bilevel optimization problem

minx∈ℝdx⁡Φ⁡(x):=f⁡(x,y⋆​(x)),y⋆​(x):=arg​miny∈ℝdy⁡g​(x,y),\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}}\ \Phi(x):=f(x,y^{\star}(x)),\qquad y^{\star}(x):=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}}g(x,y), (3)

where ff and gg are the upper- and lower-level objectives, respectively. We use the notation

H⁡(x,y):=∇y​y2g​(x,y),J⁡(x,y):=∇x​y2g​(x,y),b⁡(x,y):=∇yf​(x,y).H(x,y):=\nabla^{2}_{yy}g(x,y),\qquad J(x,y):=\nabla^{2}_{xy}g(x,y),\qquad b(x,y):=\nabla_{y}f(x,y).

Thus H⁡(x,y)∈ℝdy×dyH(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}\times d_{y}} and J⁡(x,y)∈ℝdx×dyJ(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}\times d_{y}}, so both matrices act on vectors in ℝdy\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}. We define the auxiliary linear-system solutions at a generic point (x,y)(x,y) and at the lower-level minimizer, respectively, as

z⁡(x,y):=H​(x,y)−1​b​(x,y),z⋆​(x):=z⁡(x,y⋆​(x)).z(x,y):=H(x,y)^{-1}b(x,y),\qquad z^{\star}(x):=z(x,y^{\star}(x)).

Under Assumption 2.1 below, H⁡(x,y)⪰μ​IH(x,y)\succeq\mu I, and implicit differentiation yields the hypergradient

∇Φ​(x)=∇xf​(x,y⋆​(x))−J⁡(x,y⋆​(x))​z⋆​(x).\nabla\Phi(x)=\nabla_{x}f(x,y^{\star}(x))-J(x,y^{\star}(x))z^{\star}(x). (4)

Our goal is to find an approximately stationary point of Φ\Phi. For a possibly random output xRx_{R}, we refer to 𝔼​‖∇Φ​(xR)‖2≤ϵ2\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\nabla\Phi(x_{R})\right\rVert^{2}\leq{\epsilon}^{2} as an ϵ{\epsilon}-stationarity guarantee.

2.1 Assumptions

We study smooth nonconvex–strongly-convex (NC–SC) bilevel optimization under the following regularity assumptions.

Assumption 2.1 (Base NC–SC regularity).

The following conditions hold for constants ℓf,ℓg,ρ1,μ>0\ell_{f},\ell_{g},\rho_{1},\mu>0:

  1. (i)

    ff is differentiable with a jointly ℓf\ell_{f}-Lipschitz gradient, and gg is twice differentiable with a jointly ℓg\ell_{g}-Lipschitz gradient.

  2. (ii)

    g⁡(x,⋅)g(x,\cdot) is μ\mu-strongly convex for every xx.

  3. (iii)

    The Hessian block ∇y​y2​g\nabla^{2}_{yy}g and the mixed derivative ∇x​y2​g\nabla^{2}_{xy}g are each ρ1\rho_{1}-Lipschitz in the joint variable (x,y)(x,y) with respect to the operator norm.

  4. (iv)

    ‖∇yf​(x,y)‖≤Bf\left\lVert\nabla_{y}f(x,y)\right\rVert\leq B_{f} for all (x,y)(x,y), and Φ\Phi is bounded below.

These assumptions are standard in the literature (Kwon et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026a) and are weaker than those used in some prior work (Kwon et al., 2023). Assumption 2.1 implies that, for every (x,y)(x,y),

‖z⁡(x,y)‖≤Bf/μ,‖z⋆​(x)‖≤Bf/μ.\left\lVert z(x,y)\right\rVert\leq B_{f}/\mu,\qquad\left\lVert z^{\star}(x)\right\rVert\leq B_{f}/\mu.

We define the closed Euclidean ball centered at the origin with radius RzR_{z} by

Q:={z∈ℝdy:‖z‖≤Rz},Rz:=4​Bf/μ.Q:=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}:\left\lVert z\right\rVert\leq R_{z}\},\qquad R_{z}:=4B_{f}/\mu.

The algorithm will project its auxiliary updates onto QQ. This choice of radius ensures that both the current-point linear-system solution z⁡(x,y)z(x,y) and the target z⋆​(x)z^{\star}(x) lie in QQ.

Assumption 2.2 (Lower-variable order-pp smoothness).

Fix an integer p≥1p\geq 1 and a constant Lp>0L_{p}>0. For each ℓ∈{x,y}\ell\in\{x,y\}, the map ∇ℓg​(x,⋅)\nabla_{\ell}g(x,\cdot) is pp times differentiable for every xx and satisfies

‖∇yp​∇ℓg​(x,y)−∇yp​∇ℓg​(x,y′)‖op≤Lp​‖y−y′‖, for all ​x,y,y′.\left\lVert\nabla_{y}^{p}\nabla_{\ell}g(x,y)-\nabla_{y}^{p}\nabla_{\ell}g(x,y^{\prime})\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq L_{p}\left\lVert y-y^{\prime}\right\rVert,\text{ for all }x,y,y^{\prime}. (5)

This assumption imposes order-pp smoothness on the gradients of the lower-level objective with respect to the lower variable. For p=1p=1, it follows from Assumption 2.1(iii) with L1=ρ1L_{1}=\rho_{1}, recovering the standard setting. Beyond the base regularity conditions, we impose an explicit Lipschitz condition only at order pp, without separately imposing such conditions at each intermediate derivative order. The additional higher-order condition concerns only gg; in contrast, prior work also imposes higher-order smoothness on ff with respect to yy (Chen et al., 2026b).

2.2 Stochastic gradient oracle

We now specify the stochastic gradient oracle used for both the upper and lower complexity bounds. At a query point (x,y)(x,y), a single oracle call returns four gradient estimates:

𝒪⁡(x,y)=(F^x​(x,y),F^y​(x,y),G^x​(x,y),G^y​(x,y)).\mathcal{O}(x,y)=\bigl(\hat{F}_{x}(x,y),\hat{F}_{y}(x,y),\hat{G}_{x}(x,y),\hat{G}_{y}(x,y)\bigr).

For ℓ∈{x,y}\ell\in\{x,y\}, F^ℓ​(x,y)\hat{F}_{\ell}(x,y) estimates ∇ℓf​(x,y)\nabla_{\ell}f(x,y), and G^ℓ​(x,y)\hat{G}_{\ell}(x,y) estimates ∇ℓg​(x,y)\nabla_{\ell}g(x,y). These estimates are assumed to be unbiased and to have bounded variance, as specified below.

Assumption 2.3 (Unbiased oracle with bounded variance).

The query rules and oracle responses are measurable. Let ℋ\mathcal{H} denote the history before an oracle call, and let (x,y)(x,y) be an ℋ\mathcal{H}-measurable query point. For each ℓ∈{x,y}\ell\in\{x,y\}, the returned estimates satisfy

𝔼⁡[F^ℓ​(x,y)∣ℋ]=∇ℓf​(x,y),𝔼⁡[G^ℓ​(x,y)∣ℋ]=∇ℓg​(x,y),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\hat{F}_{\ell}(x,y)\mid\mathcal{H}]=\nabla_{\ell}f(x,y),\qquad\mathbb{E}[\hat{G}_{\ell}(x,y)\mid\mathcal{H}]=\nabla_{\ell}g(x,y), (6)
∑ℓ∈{x,y}𝔼⁡[‖F^ℓ​(x,y)−∇ℓf​(x,y)‖2+‖G^ℓ​(x,y)−∇ℓg​(x,y)‖2|ℋ]≤σ2,\displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in\{x,y\}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\hat{F}_{\ell}(x,y)-\nabla_{\ell}f(x,y)\|^{2}+\|\hat{G}_{\ell}(x,y)-\nabla_{\ell}g(x,y)\|^{2}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{H}\right]\leq\sigma^{2}, (7)

almost surely, for a constant σ≥0\sigma\geq 0. Each call uses fresh randomness. Calls at query points fixed by a common conditioning history are conditionally independent given that history. No independence is assumed among the four estimates F^x,F^y,G^x,G^y\hat{F}_{x},\hat{F}_{y},\hat{G}_{x},\hat{G}_{y} returned by a single call.

For the upper-bound analysis, we use the following shorthand for minibatch estimates obtained by averaging mm fresh oracle calls at a fixed query point (x,y)(x,y):

F¯ℓ​(x,y):=1m​∑i=1mF^ℓ,i​(x,y),G¯ℓ​(x,y):=1m​∑i=1mG^ℓ,i​(x,y),ℓ∈{x,y}.\bar{F}_{\ell}(x,y):=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\hat{F}_{\ell,i}(x,y),\qquad\bar{G}_{\ell}(x,y):=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\hat{G}_{\ell,i}(x,y),\qquad\ell\in\{x,y\}.

3 A Single-Loop First-Order Algorithm

In this section, we introduce our single-loop first-order algorithm and establish its convergence guarantee. We begin with a finite-difference procedure for estimating the matrix–vector products appearing in (4), together with the bias and variance of the finite-difference approximation.

3.1 Estimating matrix–vector products from first-order queries

We approximate the indirect term in (4) by tracking z⋆​(x)z^{\star}(x) and forming J⁡(x,y)​zJ(x,y)z. At an available pair (x,y)(x,y), the tracking update for zz is driven by the linear-system residual H⁡(x,y)​z−b⁡(x,y)H(x,y)z-b(x,y). Thus, both H⁡(x,y)​zH(x,y)z and J⁡(x,y)​zJ(x,y)z must be estimated using only first-order information.

For z≠0z\neq 0, define u:=z/‖z‖u:=z/\|z\|, and set u:=0u:=0 when z=0z=0. The two matrix–vector products admit the directional-derivative representations

H⁡(x,y)​z\displaystyle H(x,y)z =‖z‖​limt→0∇yg​(x,y+t​u)−∇yg​(x,y−t​u)2​t,\displaystyle=\|z\|\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{\nabla_{y}g(x,y+tu)-\nabla_{y}g(x,y-tu)}{2t}, (8)
J⁡(x,y)​z\displaystyle J(x,y)z =‖z‖​limt→0∇xg​(x,y+t​u)−∇xg​(x,y−t​u)2​t.\displaystyle=\|z\|\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{\nabla_{x}g(x,y+tu)-\nabla_{x}g(x,y-tu)}{2t}. (9)

Evaluating these quotients at a finite radius τ>0\tau>0 yields a first-order finite-difference approximation. For example, H⁡(x,y)​z≈‖z‖2​τ​[∇yg​(x,y+τ​u)−∇yg​(x,y−τ​u)],H(x,y)z\ \approx\ \frac{\|z\|}{2\tau}\bigl[\nabla_{y}g(x,y+\tau u)-\nabla_{y}g(x,y-\tau u)\bigr], and replacing ∇yg\nabla_{y}g by ∇xg\nabla_{x}g gives the corresponding approximation of J⁡(x,y)​zJ(x,y)z.

To exploit the higher-order regularity in Assumption 2.2, we use a higher-order finite-difference stencil that combines gradients evaluated at several points y+j​τ​uy+j\tau u along the same line. Such interpolation-based finite-difference formulas are classical; see, e.g., (Atkinson and Han, 2001; Khan and Ohba, 1999; Fornberg, 1988). Let ℐ1={−1,1},\mathcal{I}_{1}=\{-1,1\}, and, for p≥2p\geq 2, let ℐp={−⌊p/2⌋,…,⌈p/2⌉}.\mathcal{I}_{p}=\{-\lfloor p/2\rfloor,\ldots,\lceil p/2\rceil\}. Choose the unique interpolation weights {aj}j∈ℐp\{a_{j}\}_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{p}} satisfying

∑j∈ℐpaj=0,∑j∈ℐpjaj=1,∑j∈ℐpjraj=0(2≤r≤p).\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{p}}a_{j}=0,\qquad\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{p}}ja_{j}=1,\qquad\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{p}}j^{r}a_{j}=0\quad(2\leq r\leq p). (10)

These moment conditions preserve the first-order term in the Taylor expansion while canceling all polynomial terms of orders 0,2,…,p0,2,\ldots,p.

For ℓ∈{x,y}\ell\in\{x,y\}, define

FDℓ​(x,y,z):=‖z‖τ​∑j∈ℐpaj​∇ℓg​(x,y+j​τ​u).\mathrm{FD}_{\ell}(x,y;z):=\frac{\|z\|}{\tau}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{p}}a_{j}\nabla_{\ell}g(x,y+j\tau u). (11)

We suppress the dependence on pp and τ\tau in the notation. For p=1p=1 and p=2p=2, the zero coefficients can be omitted, and (11) reduces to the same two-point central difference. For every pp, the stencil contains at most p+1p+1 query locations. A similar high-order finite-difference construction is used by Chen et al. (2026b), but for a different purpose. Their differences are applied to quantities arising from perturbed lower-level problems within a penalty-based construction, whereas our differences act directly on the original lower-level gradients along the direction zz to estimate the actions H​zHz and J​zJz.

Stochastic estimates.

At each node j∈ℐpj\in\mathcal{I}_{p}, we average mm fresh observations of G^ℓ\hat{G}_{\ell} into G¯ℓ,j\bar{G}_{\ell,j}, using separate batches across nodes. We then define the stochastic finite-difference estimator

FD^ℓ​(x,y,z):=‖z‖τ​∑j∈ℐpaj​G¯ℓ,j​(x,y+j​τ​u).\widehat{\mathrm{FD}}_{\ell}(x,y;z):=\frac{\|z\|}{\tau}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{p}}a_{j}\bar{G}_{\ell,j}(x,y+j\tau u). (12)

Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be a history that fixes (x,y,z)(x,y,z) before these batches are drawn. Then

𝔼⁡[FD^ℓ​(x,y,z)∣ℋ]=FDℓ​(x,y,z).\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{FD}}_{\ell}(x,y;z)\mid\mathcal{H}]=\mathrm{FD}_{\ell}(x,y;z).

Define Ap:=∑j∈ℐpaj2A_{p}:=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{p}}a_{j}^{2}. Under Assumptions 2.2 and 2.3, for each ℓ∈{x,y}\ell\in\{x,y\},

‖FDℓ​(x,y,z)−∇ℓ​y2g​(x,y)​z‖≤Cp​Lp​τp​‖z‖,\displaystyle\|\mathrm{FD}_{\ell}(x,y;z)-\nabla_{\ell y}^{2}g(x,y)z\|\leq C_{p}L_{p}\tau^{p}\|z\|, (13)
𝔼⁡[‖FD^ℓ​(x,y,z)−FDℓ​(x,y,z)‖2|ℋ]≤Ap​σ2​‖z‖2m​τ2,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\widehat{\mathrm{FD}}_{\ell}(x,y;z)-\mathrm{FD}_{\ell}(x,y;z)\|^{2}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{H}\right]\leq\frac{A_{p}\sigma^{2}\|z\|^{2}}{m\tau^{2}}, (14)

where CpC_{p} depends only on the stencil nodes and weights. Explicit expressions for CpC_{p} and ApA_{p} are given in Lemma A.3. Related expressions follow from classical finite-difference formulas; see, e.g., Li (2005); Bai et al. (2009). For completeness, we provide a self-contained proof in the appendix.

Equations (13) and (14) reveal the bias–variance tradeoff induced by finite differencing. A smaller τ\tau decreases the deterministic bias at rate τp\tau^{p}, but amplifies the stochastic variance at rate τ−2\tau^{-2}. Increasing the batch size mm controls this variance amplification. The dependence of CpC_{p} and ApA_{p} on the stencil therefore enters the constants in the resulting complexity bounds.

3.2 Algorithm

We present our algorithm, Moving-Target Tracking with Finite Differences (MRT-FD), in Algorithm 1. The intuition behind the single-loop design is similar to that of SOBA (Dagréou et al., 2022): rather than solving the lower-level problem and the auxiliary linear system to high accuracy at every outer iteration, the algorithm maintains and updates the variables xx, yy, and zz simultaneously. Compared with SOBA, MRT-FD requires only an unbiased, bounded-variance first-order oracle. Finite differences replace Hessian- and Jacobian-vector products without requiring samplewise smoothness or sample reuse across query points. Projection controls the resulting estimation errors.

The xx update: estimate the outer gradient.

The outer update uses a stochastic approximation of ∇Φ​(xk)\nabla\Phi(x_{k}). In (4), replacing the unavailable y⋆​(xk)y^{\star}(x_{k}) and z⋆​(xk)z^{\star}(x_{k}) by the current lower iterate yky_{k} and the newly updated auxiliary iterate zk+1z_{k+1} gives

∇xf​(xk,yk)−J⁡(xk,yk)​zk+1.\nabla_{x}f(x_{k},y_{k})-J(x_{k},y_{k})z_{k+1}. (15)

The two terms in (15) are estimated by F¯x,k:=F¯x​(xk,yk)\bar{F}_{x,k}:=\bar{F}_{x}(x_{k},y_{k}) and FD^x​(xk,yk,zk+1)\widehat{\mathrm{FD}}_{x}(x_{k},y_{k};z_{k+1}), respectively. Accordingly, define h^k:=F¯x,k−FD^x​(xk,yk,zk+1)\hat{h}_{k}:=\bar{F}_{x,k}-\widehat{\mathrm{FD}}_{x}(x_{k},y_{k};z_{k+1}) to approximate hypergradient, and then the outer update can be written as xk+1=xk−ηx​h^kx_{k+1}=x_{k}-\eta_{x}\hat{h}_{k}. The discrepancy between h^k\hat{h}_{k} and ∇Φ​(xk)\nabla\Phi(x_{k}) comes from four sources: the tracking errors of yky_{k} and zk+1z_{k+1}, the finite-difference bias, and the stochastic sampling noise. The yy- and zz-updates are designed to control the two tracking errors. Since the outer iterate xkx_{k} changes over time, the corresponding targets y⋆​(xk)y^{\star}(x_{k}) and z⋆​(xk)z^{\star}(x_{k}) also evolve; MRT-FD therefore treats them as moving targets.

The zz update: track the inverse-Hessian–gradient product.

At the available pair (xk,yk)(x_{k},y_{k}), the vector z⁡(xk,yk)z(x_{k},y_{k}) minimizes the strongly convex quadratic

z⟼12​z⊤​H​(xk,yk)​z−b​(xk,yk)⊤​z.z\ \longmapsto\ \tfrac{1}{2}z^{\top}H(x_{k},y_{k})z-b(x_{k},y_{k})^{\top}z. (16)

The gradient of this quadratic is the linear-system residual H⁡(xk,yk)​z−b⁡(xk,yk)H(x_{k},y_{k})z-b(x_{k},y_{k}), whose unique zero is z⁡(xk,yk)z(x_{k},y_{k}). Moreover, z⁡(xk,yk)z(x_{k},y_{k}) approaches the target z⋆​(xk)z^{\star}(x_{k}) as yky_{k} approaches y⋆​(xk)y^{\star}(x_{k}). With F¯y,k:=F¯y​(xk,yk)\bar{F}_{y,k}:=\bar{F}_{y}(x_{k},y_{k}), Line 3 estimates the residual at zkz_{k} using FD^y​(xk,yk,zk)−F¯y,k\widehat{\mathrm{FD}}_{y}(x_{k},y_{k};z_{k})-\bar{F}_{y,k} and performs one projected stochastic gradient step. Since ‖z⁡(xk,yk)‖≤Bf/μ\|z(x_{k},y_{k})\|\leq B_{f}/\mu, choosing Rz≥Bf/μR_{z}\geq B_{f}/\mu ensures that the current linear-system solution lies in QQ. The projection also guarantees ‖zk‖≤Rz\|z_{k}\|\leq R_{z} for every kk, which is crucial for uniformly controlling the finite-difference bias and variance in (13)–(14).

The yy update: track the lower solution.

With G¯y,k:=G¯y​(xk,yk)\bar{G}_{y,k}:=\bar{G}_{y}(x_{k},y_{k}), Line 5 performs one stochastic gradient step on g⁡(xk,⋅)g(x_{k},\cdot) at yky_{k}, namely yk+1=yk−ηy​G¯y,ky_{k+1}=y_{k}-\eta_{y}\bar{G}_{y,k}, to track y⋆​(xk)y^{\star}(x_{k}). This tracking controls the evaluation-point error in both the outer direction and the coefficients H⁡(xk,yk)H(x_{k},y_{k}) and b⁡(xk,yk)b(x_{k},y_{k}) of the auxiliary linear system.

3.3 Convergence guarantee

Let Φinf:=infxΦ⁡(x)\Phi_{\inf}:=\inf_{x}\Phi(x), and let Δ0\Delta_{0} denote an upper bound on the initial objective gap and tracking errors:

Δ0≥Φ⁡(x0)−Φinf+‖y0−y⋆​(x0)‖2+(Bf/μ)2,\Delta_{0}\geq\Phi(x_{0})-\Phi_{\inf}+\|y_{0}-y^{\star}(x_{0})\|^{2}+(B_{f}/\mu)^{2},

where the last term bounds the squared auxiliary tracking error at z0=0z_{0}=0. Let α>0\alpha>0 and C⋆≥1C_{\star}\geq 1 be the constants specified in Theorem 3.1. We set the projection radius to Rz=4​Bf/μR_{z}=4B_{f}/\mu, choose the tracking stepsizes ηy=ηz=1/(2​ℓg)\eta_{y}=\eta_{z}=1/(2\ell_{g}), and set the outer stepsize ηx=α\eta_{x}=\alpha. For a target accuracy 0<ϵ≤10<{\epsilon}\leq 1, choose the finite-difference radius, minibatch size, and number of iterations as

τ=(ϵ23​C⋆)1/(2​p),m=⌈3​C⋆ϵ2​τ2⌉,K=⌈3​C⋆​(1+Δ0)ϵ2⌉.\tau=\left(\frac{{\epsilon}^{2}}{3C_{\star}}\right)^{1/(2p)},\qquad m=\left\lceil\frac{3C_{\star}}{{\epsilon}^{2}\tau^{2}}\right\rceil,\qquad K=\left\lceil\frac{3C_{\star}(1+\Delta_{0})}{{\epsilon}^{2}}\right\rceil. (17)

The role of the smoothness order pp is apparent from these choices. Since the finite-difference bias scales as τ2​p\tau^{2p}, a larger pp allows a larger difference radius τ\tau while maintaining the same target bias. This reduces the variance amplification 1/τ21/\tau^{2} and, consequently, the required minibatch size mm. The resulting convergence and oracle complexity are summarized below.

Theorem 3.1.

Suppose Assumptions 2.1–2.3 hold. There exist constants α>0\alpha>0 and C⋆≥1C_{\star}\geq 1, depending only on pp and ℓf,ℓg,ρ1,μ,Bf,Lp,σ\ell_{f},\ell_{g},\rho_{1},\mu,B_{f},L_{p},\sigma, such that the following holds. Run Algorithm 1 from fixed x0,y0x_{0},y_{0} and z0=0z_{0}=0, with Rz=4​Bf/μR_{z}=4B_{f}/\mu, ηy=ηz=1/(2​ℓg)\eta_{y}=\eta_{z}=1/(2\ell_{g}), and ηx=α\eta_{x}=\alpha. For any 0<τ≤10<\tau\leq 1 and positive integers m,Km,K, the output satisfies

𝔼​‖∇Φ​(xR)‖2≤C⋆​(Δ0K+τ2​p+1m​τ2).\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi(x_{R})\|^{2}\leq C_{\star}\left(\frac{\Delta_{0}}{K}+\tau^{2p}+\frac{1}{m\tau^{2}}\right). (18)

With the parameter choices in (17), we obtain 𝔼​‖∇Φ​(xR)‖2≤ϵ2\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi(x_{R})\|^{2}\leq{\epsilon}^{2} using at most

(2​p+5)​m​K=𝒪⁡(ϵ−4−2/p)(2p+5)mK=\mathcal{O}\!\left({\epsilon}^{-4-2/p}\right)

oracle calls, for any fixed finite pp.

Appendix A provides the proof and explicit admissible choices of α\alpha and C⋆C_{\star}. For p=1p=1, Theorem 3.1 gives an 𝒪⁡(ϵ−6)\mathcal{O}({\epsilon}^{-6}) sample complexity, matching existing upper bounds (Chen et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2026a). The single-loop method of Gu et al. (2026b) attains the same dependence under additional boundedness assumptions. For p≥2p\geq 2, our rate matches the ϵ−4−2/p{\epsilon}^{-4-2/p} dependence of Chen et al. (2026b) while removing the logarithmic factor. Moreover, Chen et al. (2026b) assumes higher-order smoothness of both ff and gg in yy, as their finite-difference estimator is applied to the gradient of a penalty function that combines the upper- and lower-level objectives.

4 Matching Lower Bound under First-Order Oracles

We first recall a hard instance construction for stochastic nonconvex minimization and establish its lower bound under a stronger oracle notion. We then lift this construction to a bilevel instance and show that the bilevel oracle call can be simulated by the oracle in the minimization hard instance.

4.1 A stochastic nonconvex minimization hard instance

Consider a smooth objective P:ℝd→ℝP:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} whose gradient Lipschitz constant is bounded by a numerical constant and P⁡(0)−infP≤1P(0)-\inf P\leq 1. An ordinary stochastic-gradient oracle returns ∇P^​(x)\widehat{\nabla P}(x) such that, for each query xx selected from the history ℋ\mathcal{H},

𝔼⁡[∇P^​(x)∣ℋ]=∇P​(x),𝔼⁡[‖∇P^​(x)−∇P​(x)‖2∣ℋ]≤1.\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\nabla P}(x)\mid\mathcal{H}]=\nabla P(x),\qquad\mathbb{E}[\|\widehat{\nabla P}(x)-\nabla P(x)\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{H}]\leq 1.

The construction below recovers the standard minimization lower bound under a strengthened oracle and provides the functions and mechanism used later in our bilevel hard instance.

The objective and its decomposition.

The standard smooth chain CT​(v)=∑i=1Tψi​(v)C_{T}(v)=\sum_{i=1}^{T}\psi_{i}(v), v∈ℝTv\in\mathbb{R}^{T}, couples neighboring coordinates: each ψi\psi_{i} depends only on (vi−1,vi)(v_{i-1},v_{i}), with v0=1v_{0}=1 (Carmon et al., 2020). At a point supported on the first kk coordinates, its gradient is supported on at most the first k+1k+1. Moreover, |vT|≤1|v_{T}|\leq 1 implies ‖∇CT​(v)‖≥1\|\nabla C_{T}(v)\|\geq 1. Thus a small gradient requires reaching the last coordinate, while gradients expose at most one new coordinate at a time along such queries.

Following (Arjevani et al., 2023), we introduce smooth weights Θi​(v)∈[0,1]\Theta_{i}(v)\in[0,1] to isolate the component that can reveal the next coordinate:

WT(v):=−∑i=1TΘi(v)ψi(v),BT(v):=CT(v)+WT(v).W_{T}(v):=-\sum_{i=1}^{T}\Theta_{i}(v)\psi_{i}(v),\qquad B_{T}(v):=C_{T}(v)+W_{T}(v). (19)

The weight Θi\Theta_{i} equals one if |vj|≤1/4|v_{j}|\leq 1/4 for every j≥ij\geq i, and zero if some |vj|≥1/2|v_{j}|\geq 1/2 with j≥ij\geq i. For queries supported on the first kk coordinates, ∇BT\nabla B_{T} stays within those coordinates, whereas ∇WT\nabla W_{T} can reach coordinate k+1k+1. The specific weights also keep WTW_{T}, its gradient, and its Hessian bounded independently of TT. Appendix B.1 gives the formulas for ψi,Θi\psi_{i},\Theta_{i} and proves these properties.

Choose T=Θ⁡(ϵ−2)T=\Theta({\epsilon}^{-2}) and numerical scalings a=Θ⁡(ϵ2)a=\Theta({\epsilon}^{2}) and λlb=Θ⁡(ϵ)\lambda_{\rm lb}=\Theta({\epsilon}). Let U∈ℝd×TU\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times T} satisfy U⊤​U=ITU^{\top}U=I_{T}; in the lower-bound argument, UU is drawn uniformly at random to hide the chain directions from an adaptive algorithm (Arjevani et al., 2023; Woodworth and Srebro, 2017). Define the soft compression map

ρR​(w):=w1+‖w‖2/R2,R=230​T,\rho_{R}(w):=\frac{w}{\sqrt{1+\|w\|^{2}/R^{2}}},\qquad R=230\sqrt{T},

and the corresponding latent coordinate v⁡(x):=U⊤​ρR​(x/λlb)v(x):=U^{\top}\rho_{R}(x/\lambda_{\rm lb}). The hard objective and the pair (A,u)(A,u) are

P⁡(x)\displaystyle P(x) :=a​CT​(v⁡(x))+a10​λlb2​‖x‖2,\displaystyle:=aC_{T}(v(x))+\frac{a}{10\lambda_{\rm lb}^{2}}\|x\|^{2}, (20)
u⁡(x)\displaystyle u(x) :=aWT(v(x)),A(x):=P(x)+u(x).\displaystyle:=aW_{T}(v(x)),\qquad A(x):=P(x)+u(x).

Here u:ℝd→ℝu:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} carries the next-coordinate information and P=A−uP=A-u. The soft compression bounds the points seen by the chain, while the quadratic term prevents large-norm queries from having a small gradient. Although A,u,PA,u,P depend on the chosen UU through v⁡(x)v(x), we omit this dependence from the notation. Appendix B.2 verifies the scaling constants.

The gradient oracle and a comparison oracle.

At each call, draw a fresh ζ∼Bernoulli⁡(ϖ)\zeta\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\varpi) and define the stochastic gradient estimator

∇P^(x):=∇A(x)−ζϖ∇u(x).\widehat{\nabla P}(x):=\nabla A(x)-\frac{\zeta}{\varpi}\nabla u(x). (21)

Since 𝔼⁡[ζ/ϖ]=1\mathbb{E}[\zeta/\varpi]=1, this estimator is unbiased, while the informative correction ∇u​(x)\nabla u(x) is suppressed with probability 1−ϖ1-\varpi. For the lower-bound argument, we introduce a richer oracle response,

ℛϖ(x):=(∇A(x),ζϖu(x),ζϖ∇u(x)),\mathcal{R}_{\varpi}(x):=\left(\nabla A(x),\frac{\zeta}{\varpi}u(x),\frac{\zeta}{\varpi}\nabla u(x)\right), (22)

which we call the comparison oracle. It is stronger than (21), since subtracting its third component from its first recovers the stochastic gradient estimate in one call. The additional scalar component ζϖ​u​(x)\frac{\zeta}{\varpi}u(x) is included because it will be used to reproduce the lower-gradient oracle G^y\hat{G}_{y} in the bilevel construction. The next proposition establishes a lower bound directly for this stronger oracle.

Proposition 4.1 (Hard objective and comparison oracle).

There are numerical constants c,C,ϵ0>0c,C,{\epsilon}_{0}>0 such that, for every 0<ϵ<ϵ00<{\epsilon}<{\epsilon}_{0} and 0<ϖ≤1/20<\varpi\leq 1/2, the construction (20) admits T=Θ⁡(ϵ−2)T=\Theta({\epsilon}^{-2}), d≥Td\geq T, and a distribution of UU with the following properties. Both ∇A\nabla A and ∇u\nabla u are CC-Lipschitz, P⁡(0)−infP≤1/4P(0)-\inf P\leq 1/4, and

supx|u⁡(x)|≤C​ϵ2,supx‖∇u​(x)‖≤C​ϵ.\sup_{x}|u(x)|\leq C{\epsilon}^{2},\qquad\sup_{x}\|\nabla u(x)\|\leq C{\epsilon}. (23)

Every adaptive randomized algorithm using at most c​T/ϖcT/\varpi calls to ℛϖ\mathcal{R}_{\varpi}, with arbitrary queries and final output, satisfies

ℙ⁡(‖∇P​(xout)‖≥2​ϵ)≥34.\mathbb{P}\bigl(\|\nabla P(x_{\rm out})\|\geq 2{\epsilon}\bigr)\geq\frac{3}{4}. (24)

The rotation UU is independent of the algorithm seed and oracle draws; probability includes all three sources of randomness.

The two vector responses in ℛϖ\mathcal{R}_{\varpi} arise from U∇BT(v)U\nabla B_{T}(v) and U(ζ/ϖ)∇WT(v)U(\zeta/\varpi)\nabla W_{T}(v). Along an exposed coordinate prefix, these vectors can add at most one direction, and only when ζ=1\zeta=1 (Corollary B.3), giving a mean waiting time 1/ϖ1/\varpi between opportunities for progress. For arbitrary queries, the proof conditions on the past latent coordinates v⁡(xt)v(x_{t}), oracle draws, and exposed directions, which together determine all past scalar responses. The residual parts of unrevealed directions orthogonal to past queries and exposed directions remain spherically symmetric, allowing high-dimensional concentration to control accidental progress (Lemmas B.11–B.13). The same geometric bound covers the final output as an additional point without an oracle call (Corollary B.14). Appendix B.4 gives the full proof.

Choosing ϖ=2​(1+C2)​ϵ2\varpi=2(1+C^{2}){\epsilon}^{2} recovers the classical Ω⁡(ϵ−4)\Omega({\epsilon}^{-4}) lower bound for stochastic nonconvex minimization under an ordinary first-order oracle; see Appendix B.4.1. More importantly, the comparison-oracle construction enables a stronger bilevel lower bound: after lifting the hard instance to a bilevel problem, we can choose a even smaller reveal probability ϖ\varpi while preserving bounded variance, which increases the number of oracle calls required.

4.2 A bilevel hard instance

We use the same pair (A,u)(A,u) to construct a bilevel hard instance and its primitive first-order oracle. For a scale ϵ≤δ≤1{\epsilon}\leq\delta\leq 1, let x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and let the lower-level variable be scalar, y∈ℝy\in\mathbb{R}. Define the upper- and lower-level objectives by

fδ​(x,y):=A⁡(x)+y,gδ​(x,y):=12​y2+δ​sin⁡(y/δ)​u​(x).f_{\delta}(x,y):=A(x)+y,\qquad g_{\delta}(x,y):=\tfrac{1}{2}y^{2}+\delta\sin(y/\delta)u(x). (25)

At a query point (x,y)(x,y), draw one response from the comparison oracle, (r1,r2,r3)=ℛϖ(x)=(∇A(x),ζϖu(x),ζϖ∇u(x))(r_{1},r_{2},r_{3})=\mathcal{R}_{\varpi}(x)=\left(\nabla A(x),\frac{\zeta}{\varpi}u(x),\frac{\zeta}{\varpi}\nabla u(x)\right), and transform it into the primitive bilevel oracle response:

F^x=r1,F^y=1,G^x=δ​sin⁡(y/δ)​r3,G^y=y+cos⁡(y/δ)​r2.\hat{F}_{x}=r_{1},\qquad\hat{F}_{y}=1,\qquad\hat{G}_{x}=\delta\sin(y/\delta)r_{3},\qquad\hat{G}_{y}=y+\cos(y/\delta)r_{2}. (26)

These are exactly the stochastic gradients of fδf_{\delta} and gδg_{\delta}, with the same Bernoulli variable ζ\zeta appearing in both lower-level gradient blocks. Hence, one comparison-oracle call exactly simulates one primitive bilevel oracle call, including its joint randomness.

The terms carrying the hidden correction uu are δsin(y/δ)∇u(x)\delta\sin(y/\delta)\nabla u(x) and cos⁡(y/δ)​u​(x)\cos(y/\delta)u(x). Their joint norm is O⁡(δ​ϵ)O(\delta{\epsilon}) uniformly over (x,y)(x,y), since ‖∇u‖=O⁡(ϵ)\|\nabla u\|=O({\epsilon}), |u|=O⁡(ϵ2)|u|=O({\epsilon}^{2}), and δ≥ϵ\delta\geq{\epsilon}. We refer to this quantity as the signal size: it measures the magnitude of the deterministic terms involving uu before multiplication by ζ/ϖ\zeta/\varpi. These terms contain the information needed to recover the correction −∇u-\nabla u in ∇P=∇A−∇u\nabla P=\nabla A-\nabla u.

The hyperobjective is Φδ​(x)=A⁡(x)+yδ⋆​(x)\Phi_{\delta}(x)=A(x)+y_{\delta}^{\star}(x), where

yδ⋆+u⁡(x)​cos⁡(yδ⋆/δ)=0,|yδ⋆|≤|u⁡(x)|.y_{\delta}^{\star}+u(x)\cos(y_{\delta}^{\star}/\delta)=0,\qquad|y_{\delta}^{\star}|\leq|u(x)|.

Since |u|/δ=O⁡(ϵ)|u|/\delta=O({\epsilon}), the lower solution is close to −u-u. Implicit differentiation gives the corresponding gradient estimate. The following proposition verifies that the bilevel construction satisfies Assumption 2.1 and that its hyperobjective remains close to the hard minimization objective PP.

Proposition 4.2 (Bilevel gradient and primitive variance).

For each pair in Proposition 4.1, every ϵ≤δ≤1{\epsilon}\leq\delta\leq 1, and sufficiently small ϵ{\epsilon}, the family (25) satisfies Assumption 2.1 with uniformly bounded constants, has Φδ​(0)−infΦδ≤1\Phi_{\delta}(0)-\inf\Phi_{\delta}\leq 1 and |yδ⋆​(0)|≤1|y_{\delta}^{\star}(0)|\leq 1, and obeys

supx‖∇Φδ​(x)−∇P​(x)‖≤Clift​ϵ5/δ2≤Clift​ϵ3\sup_{x}\|\nabla\Phi_{\delta}(x)-\nabla P(x)\|\leq C_{\rm lift}{\epsilon}^{5}/\delta^{2}\leq C_{\rm lift}{\epsilon}^{3} (27)

for a numerical Clift>0C_{\rm lift}>0. The oracle (26) is conditionally unbiased, has joint variance at most Clift​δ2​ϵ2/ϖC_{\rm lift}\delta^{2}{\epsilon}^{2}/\varpi, and is simulated by one call to ℛϖ\mathcal{R}_{\varpi}.

Appendix B.5 proves the proposition. Choosing ϖδ=Θ⁡(δ2​ϵ2)\varpi_{\delta}=\Theta(\delta^{2}{\epsilon}^{2}) keeps the primitive variance at most one. On the event ‖∇P‖≥2​ϵ\|\nabla P\|\geq 2{\epsilon}, the gradient estimate gives ‖∇Φδ‖≥3​ϵ/2\|\nabla\Phi_{\delta}\|\geq 3{\epsilon}/2 for small enough ϵ{\epsilon}. The one-call simulation therefore transfers Proposition 4.1 to the bilevel objective, giving

Ω⁡(T/ϖδ)=Ω⁡(ϵ−4​δ−2)\Omega(T/\varpi_{\delta})=\Omega({\epsilon}^{-4}\delta^{-2}) (28)

primitive calls. The intuition is that the sinusoidal lower-level construction attenuates the primitive signal while preserving the relevant hypergradient information, allowing the same variance budget to support a smaller reveal probability.

4.3 Lower bound and minimax complexity

Decreasing δ\delta increases the higher-order smoothness constants of gg with respect to the lower variable. For the construction in (25), the order-pp smoothness constants in Assumption 2.2 are bounded by C​ϵ​δ−pC{\epsilon}\delta^{-p} for ℓ=x\ell=x and C​ϵ2​δ−(p+1)C{\epsilon}^{2}\delta^{-(p+1)} for ℓ=y\ell=y, where CC is a numerical constant independent of pp. Choosing δ=ϵ1/p\delta={\epsilon}^{1/p} keeps these quantities, as well as the base regularity constants, uniformly bounded. Substituting this choice into (28) yields the exponent 4+2/p4+2/p.

For M≥1M\geq 1, let 𝒫p​(M)\mathcal{P}_{p}(M) be the class of problem–oracle pairs satisfying Assumptions 2.1–2.3, in arbitrary finite dimensions, with

max⁡{ℓf,ℓg,ρ1,Lp,Bf,σ,μ−1}≤M,\displaystyle\max\{\ell_{f},\ell_{g},\rho_{1},L_{p},B_{f},\sigma,\mu^{-1}\}\leq M, (29)
Φ⁡(0)−Φinf≤1,‖y⋆​(0)‖≤1.\displaystyle\Phi(0)-\Phi_{\inf}\leq 1,\qquad\|y^{\star}(0)\|\leq 1. (30)

Queries and the final output may be arbitrary measurable functions of past oracle responses and the algorithm’s internal randomness.

Theorem 4.3 (Lower bound for bilevel problems).

There exist numerical constants M0≥1M_{0}\geq 1, c>0c>0, and ϵ0>0{\epsilon}_{0}>0 such that the following holds for every integer p≥1p\geq 1 and 0<ϵ<ϵ00<{\epsilon}<{\epsilon}_{0}. For any adaptive randomized algorithm using at most c​ϵ−4−2/pc{\epsilon}^{-4-2/p} primitive oracle calls, there is a pair in 𝒫p​(M0)\mathcal{P}_{p}(M_{0}) on which its output satisfies

𝔼​‖∇Φ​(xout)‖2>ϵ2.\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi(x_{\rm out})\|^{2}>{\epsilon}^{2}. (31)

Appendix B.6 gives the proof. The hard instances have dy=1d_{y}=1 and can be constructed with dx=O⁡(ϵ−6−2/p​log⁡(1/ϵ))d_{x}=O({\epsilon}^{-6-2/p}\log(1/{\epsilon})). Theorem 4.3 shows that the upper bound in Theorem 3.1 is tight in its dependence on ϵ{\epsilon} for every fixed finite pp and fixed problem constants.

AI use statement

We used OpenAI GPT-5.5 to assist with literature search and reference checking, manuscript drafting and revision, and selected mathematical computations and proof checking. The algorithmic design and the main convergence proof were developed by the authors; GPT-5.5 was used to help verify intermediate calculations, and improve the presentation. The initial lower-bound construction emerged through iterative discussions between the authors and GPT-5.5. The authors subsequently simplified the argument, reorganized the proof, and developed the current comparison-oracle and bilevel-lifting framework. This appendix proves the guarantee for Algorithm 1 with a common difference radius and batch size. Throughout, Assumptions 2.1–2.3 hold, and the initial points x0,y0x_{0},y_{0} are fixed with z0=0z_{0}=0.

A.2 Geometry and errors from the lower iterate

Lemma A.1 (Regularity of the lower solution and auxiliary target).

Under Assumption 2.1, the lower solution exists uniquely for every xx. Moreover,

‖y⋆​(x)−y⋆​(x′)‖\displaystyle\|y^{\star}(x)-y^{\star}(x^{\prime})\| ≤Ly​‖x−x′‖,\displaystyle\leq L_{y}\|x-x^{\prime}\|, (44)
‖z⁡(x,y)‖,‖z⋆​(x)‖\displaystyle\|z(x,y)\|,\ \|z^{\star}(x)\| ≤q0,\displaystyle\leq q_{0}, (45)
‖z⋆​(x)−z⋆​(x′)‖\displaystyle\|z^{\star}(x)-z^{\star}(x^{\prime})\| ≤Lz​‖x−x′‖.\displaystyle\leq L_{z}\|x-x^{\prime}\|. (46)

The hypergradient identity (4) holds, and ∇Φ\nabla\Phi is LΦL_{\Phi}-Lipschitz.

Proof.

Strong convexity gives a coercive quadratic lower bound for g⁡(x,⋅)g(x,\cdot), so continuity gives existence and strong convexity gives uniqueness. The first-order condition is ∇yg​(x,y⋆​(x))=0\nabla_{y}g(x,y^{\star}(x))=0. For a=y⋆​(x)a=y^{\star}(x) and a′=y⋆​(x′)a^{\prime}=y^{\star}(x^{\prime}), strong monotonicity implies

μ​‖a−a′‖2≤⟨∇yg​(x,a)−∇yg​(x,a′),a−a′⟩.\mu\|a-a^{\prime}\|^{2}\leq\langle\nabla_{y}g(x,a)-\nabla_{y}g(x,a^{\prime}),a-a^{\prime}\rangle.

Substitute the two first-order conditions and apply the Lipschitz bound in xx. The right-hand side is at most L​‖x−x′‖​‖a−a′‖L\|x-x^{\prime}\|\|a-a^{\prime}\|, proving (44), including the case a=a′a=a^{\prime}.

Differentiability of the Lipschitz gradient and lower strong convexity give

μ​I⪯H⁡(x,y)⪯L​I,‖J⁡(x,y)‖op≤L,‖H​(x,y)−1‖op≤μ−1.\mu I\preceq H(x,y)\preceq LI,\qquad\|J(x,y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq L,\qquad\|H(x,y)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\mu^{-1}.

The bound on ∇yf\nabla_{y}f now proves (45). The derivatives of (x,y)↦∇yg​(x,y)(x,y)\mapsto\nabla_{y}g(x,y) are J​(x,y)⊤J(x,y)^{\top} and H⁡(x,y)H(x,y); their continuity follows from the matrix Lipschitz bounds in Assumption 2.1(iii). The implicit-function theorem therefore applies locally at each lower solution. Uniqueness makes these local solution maps agree. It follows that

Dx​y⋆​(x)=−H​(x,y⋆​(x))−1​J​(x,y⋆​(x))⊤.D_{x}y^{\star}(x)=-H(x,y^{\star}(x))^{-1}J(x,y^{\star}(x))^{\top}.

The chain rule proves (4).

For brevity in the remaining estimates, let s=(x,y⋆​(x))s=(x,y^{\star}(x)), s′=(x′,y⋆​(x′))s^{\prime}=(x^{\prime},y^{\star}(x^{\prime})), q=z⋆​(x)q=z^{\star}(x), and q′=z⋆​(x′)q^{\prime}=z^{\star}(x^{\prime}). Subtracting the two auxiliary systems gives

H⁡(s)​(q−q′)=b⁡(s)−b⁡(s′)−[H⁡(s)−H⁡(s′)]​q′.H(s)(q-q^{\prime})=b(s)-b(s^{\prime})-[H(s)-H(s^{\prime})]q^{\prime}.

By Assumption 2.1(iii), ‖H⁡(s)−H⁡(s′)‖op≤ρ1​‖s−s′‖\|H(s)-H(s^{\prime})\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\rho_{1}\|s-s^{\prime}\|. Use this bound, ‖q′‖≤q0\|q^{\prime}\|\leq q_{0}, ‖H​(s)−1‖op≤μ−1\|H(s)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\mu^{-1}, and

‖s−s′‖≤‖x−x′‖+‖y⋆​(x)−y⋆​(x′)‖≤(1+Ly)​‖x−x′‖.\|s-s^{\prime}\|\leq\|x-x^{\prime}\|+\|y^{\star}(x)-y^{\star}(x^{\prime})\|\leq(1+L_{y})\|x-x^{\prime}\|.

The resulting bound is ‖q−q′‖≤B⁡(1+Ly)​‖x−x′‖/μ\|q-q^{\prime}\|\leq B(1+L_{y})\|x-x^{\prime}\|/\mu, proving (46).

Finally, the difference of the hypergradients equals

∇xf​(s)−∇xf​(s′)−[J⁡(s)−J⁡(s′)]​q′−J⁡(s)​(q−q′).\nabla_{x}f(s)-\nabla_{x}f(s^{\prime})-[J(s)-J(s^{\prime})]q^{\prime}-J(s)(q-q^{\prime}).

The first two terms have combined norm at most B⁡(1+Ly)​‖x−x′‖B(1+L_{y})\|x-x^{\prime}\|, and the last term has norm at most L​Lz​‖x−x′‖LL_{z}\|x-x^{\prime}\|. Their sum gives LΦL_{\Phi}. ∎

Lemma A.2 (Errors caused by the current lower iterate).

For every x,y,zx,y,z, under Assumption 2.1,

‖H⁡(x,y)​z⋆​(x)−b⁡(x,y)‖\displaystyle\|H(x,y)z^{\star}(x)-b(x,y)\| ≤B​‖y−y⋆​(x)‖,\displaystyle\leq B\|y-y^{\star}(x)\|, (47)
‖∇xf​(x,y)−J⁡(x,y)​z−∇Φ​(x)‖\displaystyle\|\nabla_{x}f(x,y)-J(x,y)z-\nabla\Phi(x)\| ≤L​‖z−z⋆​(x)‖+B​‖y−y⋆​(x)‖.\displaystyle\leq L\|z-z^{\star}(x)\|+B\|y-y^{\star}(x)\|. (48)
Proof.

Write y⋆=y⋆​(x)y^{\star}=y^{\star}(x) and q=z⋆​(x)q=z^{\star}(x). The identity H⁡(x,y⋆)​q=b⁡(x,y⋆)H(x,y^{\star})q=b(x,y^{\star}) gives

H⁡(x,y)​q−b⁡(x,y)=[H⁡(x,y)−H⁡(x,y⋆)]​q+b⁡(x,y⋆)−b⁡(x,y).H(x,y)q-b(x,y)=[H(x,y)-H(x,y^{\star})]q+b(x,y^{\star})-b(x,y).

The operator-norm Lipschitz bound on HH and ‖q‖≤q0\|q\|\leq q_{0} give the bound (ρ1​q0+ℓf)​‖y−y⋆‖(\rho_{1}q_{0}+\ell_{f})\|y-y^{\star}\|, proving (47). For the second bound, subtract (4) to obtain

∇xf​(x,y)−J⁡(x,y)​z−∇Φ​(x)\displaystyle\nabla_{x}f(x,y)-J(x,y)z-\nabla\Phi(x)
=∇xf​(x,y)−∇xf​(x,y⋆)−[J⁡(x,y)−J⁡(x,y⋆)]​q−J⁡(x,y)​(z−q).\displaystyle\quad=\nabla_{x}f(x,y)-\nabla_{x}f(x,y^{\star})-[J(x,y)-J(x,y^{\star})]q-J(x,y)(z-q).

The three terms have norms bounded respectively by ℓf​‖y−y⋆‖\ell_{f}\|y-y^{\star}\|, ρ1​q0​‖y−y⋆‖\rho_{1}q_{0}\|y-y^{\star}\|, and L​‖z−q‖L\|z-q\|. Their sum is (48). ∎

A.3 Finite differences and conditional sampling

Lemma A.3 (Normalized finite-difference error).

The weights in (10) exist uniquely for every integer p≥1p\geq 1. Under Assumptions 2.2 and 2.3, the finite differences and their sampled estimates satisfy (13)–(14) with Cp,ApC_{p},A_{p} from (33). More precisely, if x,y,zx,y,z are measurable with respect to a history ℱ\mathcal{F} and the endpoint batches use fresh calls after that history, then, for ℓ∈{x,y}\ell\in\{x,y\},

𝔼⁡[FD^ℓ​(x,y,z)∣ℱ]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{FD}}_{\ell}(x,y;z)\mid\mathcal{F}] =FDℓ​(x,y,z),\displaystyle=\mathrm{FD}_{\ell}(x,y;z), (49)
‖FDℓ​(x,y,z)−∇ℓ​y2g​(x,y)​z‖\displaystyle\|\mathrm{FD}_{\ell}(x,y;z)-\nabla^{2}_{\ell y}g(x,y)z\| ≤Cp​Lp​τp​‖z‖,\displaystyle\leq C_{p}L_{p}\tau^{p}\|z\|, (50)
𝔼⁡[‖FD^ℓ​(x,y,z)−FDℓ​(x,y,z)‖2∣ℱ]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\|\widehat{\mathrm{FD}}_{\ell}(x,y;z)-\mathrm{FD}_{\ell}(x,y;z)\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}] ≤Ap​σ2​‖z‖2m​τ2.\displaystyle\leq\frac{A_{p}\sigma^{2}\|z\|^{2}}{m\tau^{2}}. (51)

These statements include z=0z=0.

Proof.

The set ℐp\mathcal{I}_{p} has p+1p+1 distinct nodes, including for p=1p=1. Let lj​(t)l_{j}(t) be its Lagrange basis polynomials. Differentiating the interpolation identity for a polynomial of degree at most pp shows that aj=lj′​(0)a_{j}=l_{j}^{\prime}(0) satisfies (10). The Vandermonde matrix of distinct nodes is invertible, giving uniqueness.

Suppose first that z≠0z\neq 0 and condition on ℱ\mathcal{F}. Write u=z/‖z‖u=z/\|z\| and φ⁡(t)=∇ℓg​(x,y+t​u)\varphi(t)=\nabla_{\ell}g(x,y+tu). By Assumption 2.2, ∇yp​∇ℓg​(x,⋅)\nabla_{y}^{p}\nabla_{\ell}g(x,\cdot) is LpL_{p}-Lipschitz. Since ‖u‖=1\|u\|=1, the ppth derivative of φ\varphi is also LpL_{p}-Lipschitz. Taylor’s formula with an integral remainder gives, for every real tt,

φ⁡(t)\displaystyle\varphi(t) =∑r=0ptrr!​φ(r)​(0)+ℛp​(t),\displaystyle=\sum_{r=0}^{p}\frac{t^{r}}{r!}\varphi^{(r)}(0)+\mathcal{R}_{p}(t),
ℛp​(t)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{p}(t) =tp(p−1)!​∫01(1−s)p−1​[φ(p)​(s​t)−φ(p)​(0)]​𝑑s.\displaystyle=\frac{t^{p}}{(p-1)!}\int_{0}^{1}(1-s)^{p-1}[\varphi^{(p)}(st)-\varphi^{(p)}(0)]\,ds.

In particular, including when t<0t<0,

‖ℛp​(t)‖≤Lp​|t|p+1(p−1)!​∫01s​(1−s)p−1​𝑑s=Lp​|t|p+1(p+1)!.\|\mathcal{R}_{p}(t)\|\leq\frac{L_{p}|t|^{p+1}}{(p-1)!}\int_{0}^{1}s(1-s)^{p-1}\,ds=\frac{L_{p}|t|^{p+1}}{(p+1)!}.

Thus this argument does not require a (p+1)(p+1)st derivative. Insert the expansion at t=j​τt=j\tau into (11). All polynomial terms except the first derivative vanish by the moment identities. The retained term is ‖z‖​φ′​(0)=∇ℓ​y2​g​(x,y)​z\|z\|\varphi^{\prime}(0)=\nabla^{2}_{\ell y}g(x,y)z. The remainder has norm at most

‖z‖τ​∑j|aj|​Lp​|j​τ|p+1(p+1)!=Cp​Lp​τp​‖z‖.\frac{\|z\|}{\tau}\sum_{j}|a_{j}|\frac{L_{p}|j\tau|^{p+1}}{(p+1)!}=C_{p}L_{p}\tau^{p}\|z\|.

For each node jj, set νj:=G¯ℓ,j​(x,y+j​τ​u)−∇ℓg​(x,y+j​τ​u)\nu_{j}:=\bar{G}_{\ell,j}(x,y+j\tau u)-\nabla_{\ell}g(x,y+j\tau u). Every summand in (7) is nonnegative, so each block G^ℓ​(x,y)\hat{G}_{\ell}(x,y) has conditional variance at most σ2\sigma^{2}. Averaging mm independent calls reduces this bound to σ2/m\sigma^{2}/m. Together with (6), this gives

𝔼[νj∣ℱ]=0,𝔼[∥νj∥2∣ℱ]≤σ2/m,𝔼[⟨νi,νj⟩∣ℱ]=0(i≠j).\mathbb{E}[\nu_{j}\mid\mathcal{F}]=0,\qquad\mathbb{E}[\|\nu_{j}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}]\leq\sigma^{2}/m,\qquad\mathbb{E}[\langle\nu_{i},\nu_{j}\rangle\mid\mathcal{F}]=0\quad(i\neq j).

The cross terms vanish because distinct nodes use distinct calls; no independence between blocks within a single call is required. Consequently,

𝔼⁡[‖FD^ℓ−FDℓ‖2∣ℱ]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\|\widehat{\mathrm{FD}}_{\ell}-\mathrm{FD}_{\ell}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}] =‖z‖2τ2​∑jaj2​𝔼​[‖νj‖2∣ℱ]\displaystyle=\frac{\|z\|^{2}}{\tau^{2}}\sum_{j}a_{j}^{2}\mathbb{E}[\|\nu_{j}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}]
≤Ap​σ2​‖z‖2m​τ2,\displaystyle\leq\frac{A_{p}\sigma^{2}\|z\|^{2}}{m\tau^{2}},

and the same centered-noise representation proves (49). If z=0z=0, both differences and both exact matrix–vector products are zero by definition, so every assertion follows without endpoint calls. ∎

We make the sampling convention for Algorithm 1 explicit. Each occurrence of a center or node average uses a separate batch of mm fresh calls, including when query locations coincide. The zz update is sampled first. After zk+1z_{k+1} is computed, new batches are drawn for the xx update; a final fresh batch is then drawn for the yy update. All center batches are evaluated at (xk,yk)(x_{k},y_{k}), as in the algorithm. Thus the outer finite difference uses zk+1z_{k+1}, whereas the auxiliary finite difference uses zkz_{k}. At termination, the output index RR is drawn uniformly and independently of all oracle calls.

Let ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k} contain all calls before iteration kk, let ℱkz\mathcal{F}_{k}^{z} additionally contain the calls used to compute zk+1z_{k+1}, and let ℱkx\mathcal{F}_{k}^{x} additionally contain those used to compute xk+1x_{k+1}. The final lower-gradient batch completes ℱk+1\mathcal{F}_{k+1}. Thus

ℱk⊆ℱkz⊆ℱkx⊆ℱk+1.\mathcal{F}_{k}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{k}^{z}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{k}^{x}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{k+1}.

In particular, ℙ⁡(R=j∣ℱK)=1/K\mathbb{P}(R=j\mid\mathcal{F}_{K})=1/K for j=0,…,K−1j=0,\ldots,K-1. Write 𝔼k[⋅]=𝔼[⋅∣ℱk]\mathbb{E}_{k}[\cdot]=\mathbb{E}[\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}] and introduce the uniform error bounds

β:=Cp​Lp​Rz​τp,v:=σ2m​(1+Ap​Rz2τ2),vy:=σ2m≤v.\beta:=C_{p}L_{p}R_{z}\tau^{p},\qquad v:=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{m}\left(1+\frac{A_{p}R_{z}^{2}}{\tau^{2}}\right),\qquad v_{y}:=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{m}\leq v. (52)
Lemma A.4 (Conditional decomposition of the three updates).

Put Hk=H⁡(xk,yk)H_{k}=H(x_{k},y_{k}), Jk=J⁡(xk,yk)J_{k}=J(x_{k},y_{k}), and bk=b⁡(xk,yk)b_{k}=b(x_{k},y_{k}). The sampled directions in Algorithm 1 can be written as

r^k\displaystyle\hat{r}_{k} :=FD^y​(xk,yk,zk)−F¯y,k=Hk​zk−bk+dkz+ξkz,\displaystyle:=\widehat{\mathrm{FD}}_{y}(x_{k},y_{k};z_{k})-\bar{F}_{y,k}=H_{k}z_{k}-b_{k}+d_{k}^{z}+\xi_{k}^{z}, (53)
h^k\displaystyle\hat{h}_{k} =∇xf​(xk,yk)−Jk​zk+1+dkx+ξkx,\displaystyle=\nabla_{x}f(x_{k},y_{k})-J_{k}z_{k+1}+d_{k}^{x}+\xi_{k}^{x}, (54)
G¯y,k\displaystyle\bar{G}_{y,k} =∇yg​(xk,yk)+ξky.\displaystyle=\nabla_{y}g(x_{k},y_{k})+\xi_{k}^{y}. (55)

Here dkzd_{k}^{z} is ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k}-measurable, dkxd_{k}^{x} is ℱkz\mathcal{F}_{k}^{z}-measurable, and ‖dkz‖,‖dkx‖≤β\|d_{k}^{z}\|,\|d_{k}^{x}\|\leq\beta. The noises satisfy

𝔼⁡[ξkz∣ℱk]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\xi_{k}^{z}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}] =0,\displaystyle=0, 𝔼⁡[‖ξkz‖2∣ℱk]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\|\xi_{k}^{z}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}] ≤v,\displaystyle\leq v, (56)
𝔼⁡[ξkx∣ℱkz]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\xi_{k}^{x}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}^{z}] =0,\displaystyle=0, 𝔼⁡[‖ξkx‖2∣ℱkz]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\|\xi_{k}^{x}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}^{z}] ≤v,\displaystyle\leq v, (57)
𝔼⁡[ξky∣ℱkx]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\xi_{k}^{y}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}^{x}] =0,\displaystyle=0, 𝔼⁡[‖ξky‖2∣ℱkx]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\|\xi_{k}^{y}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}^{x}] ≤vy.\displaystyle\leq v_{y}. (58)
Proof.

Every zkz_{k} belongs to QQ, since z0=0z_{0}=0 and every auxiliary update is projected. Define

dkz\displaystyle d_{k}^{z} :=FDy​(xk,yk,zk)−Hk​zk,\displaystyle:=\mathrm{FD}_{y}(x_{k},y_{k};z_{k})-H_{k}z_{k},
dkx\displaystyle d_{k}^{x} :=Jk​zk+1−FDx​(xk,yk,zk+1).\displaystyle:=J_{k}z_{k+1}-\mathrm{FD}_{x}(x_{k},y_{k};z_{k+1}).

Lemma A.3 gives their measurability and bounds. Notice the opposite signs: the outer direction subtracts its finite difference.

For ξkz\xi_{k}^{z}, subtract the finite differences and exact center gradients from their sampled counterparts in r^k\hat{r}_{k}. The center term F¯y,k−bk\bar{F}_{y,k}-b_{k} is conditionally centered with variance at most σ2/m\sigma^{2}/m by the F^y\hat{F}_{y} block of (6)–(7) and fresh batching. It uses a separate batch from the finite difference, so their conditional variances add, giving at most

Ap​σ2​‖zk‖2m​τ2+σ2m≤v.\frac{A_{p}\sigma^{2}\|z_{k}\|^{2}}{m\tau^{2}}+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{m}\leq v.

For the outer direction, condition on ℱkz\mathcal{F}_{k}^{z}. Its input zk+1z_{k+1} is now fixed and lies in QQ. Entirely new center and node batches give the same argument using the F^x\hat{F}_{x} block and zk+1z_{k+1} in place of zkz_{k}. Finally, G¯y,k\bar{G}_{y,k} is drawn after ℱkx\mathcal{F}_{k}^{x} at the already selected point (xk,yk)(x_{k},y_{k}). The G^y\hat{G}_{y} block of (6)–(7) gives its conditional mean ∇yg​(xk,yk)\nabla_{y}g(x_{k},y_{k}) and variance bound vyv_{y} after averaging. These arguments also cover repeated query locations because their batches are distinct. ∎

All expectations used below are finite. To see this without assuming bounded iterates, start with the fixed x0,y0x_{0},y_{0}. The gradients of ff and gg grow at most linearly by Assumption 2.1(i), while the mean finite differences have norm at most L​Rz+βLR_{z}+\beta by Lemma A.3. The noises above have uniformly bounded second moments. Since zkz_{k} is bounded, induction through the three updates shows that xk,ykx_{k},y_{k} have finite second moments at every finite kk. Lemma A.1 then gives finite second moments for the tracking errors and the outer gradient. Finally, smoothness of Φ\Phi bounds |Φ⁡(x)||\Phi(x)| by a constant times 1+‖x‖21+\|x\|^{2}, so the objective and potential are integrable as well.

Lemma A.5 (Projected auxiliary correction at the current outer point).

With ηz=η=1/(2​L)\eta_{z}=\eta=1/(2L), the auxiliary update satisfies

𝔼k​‖e¯k‖2≤(1−r)​‖ek‖2+6​ημ​(B2​‖δk‖2+β2)+η2​v.\mathbb{E}_{k}\|\bar{e}_{k}\|^{2}\leq(1-r)\|e_{k}\|^{2}+\frac{6\eta}{\mu}\bigl(B^{2}\|\delta_{k}\|^{2}+\beta^{2}\bigr)+\eta^{2}v. (59)

𝔼k​‖e¯k‖2≤(1−r)​‖ek‖2+3​η2r​‖wk‖2+η2​v.\mathbb{E}_{k}\|\bar{e}_{k}\|^{2}\leq(1-r)\|e_{k}\|^{2}+\frac{3\eta^{2}}{r}\|w_{k}\|^{2}+\eta^{2}v.

A.5 Lyapunov descent

Proposition A.8 (A uniform one-step inequality).

Under Assumptions 2.1–2.3 and the step choices (37), for every τ>0\tau>0 and positive integer mm,

𝔼k​𝒱k+1≤𝒱k−α4​‖∇Φ​(xk)‖2−α​C​Tk+α​Sb​β2+α​Sv​v.\mathbb{E}_{k}\mathcal{V}_{k+1}\leq\mathcal{V}_{k}-\frac{\alpha}{4}\|\nabla\Phi(x_{k})\|^{2}-\alpha CT_{k}+\alpha S_{\rm b}\beta^{2}+\alpha S_{\rm v}v. (68)

All constants are given in Appendix A.1; in particular, the step sizes do not depend on the target accuracy.

Proof.

+(α​Ca2+λ​Nb)​β2+(7​α8+λ​Nv)​v.\displaystyle+\left(\frac{\alpha{C_{\rm a}}}{2}+\lambda N_{\rm b}\right)\beta^{2}+\left(\frac{7\alpha}{8}+\lambda N_{\rm v}\right)v.

Use the movement identity and (63) to bound the third term by

For an explicit check of every coefficient, put χ=C​D​α2/ρ\chi=CD\alpha^{2}/\rho. Our choice of α\alpha implies 0<χ≤1/160<\chi\leq 1/16, and λ=2​α​C/ρ\lambda=2\alpha C/\rho. Substitution yields

𝔼k​𝒱k+1−𝒱k≤\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{k}\mathcal{V}_{k+1}-\mathcal{V}_{k}\leq{} α⁡(−12+4​χ)​‖hk‖2+α​C​(−32+4​χ)​Tk\displaystyle\alpha\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}+4\chi\right)\|h_{k}\|^{2}+\alpha C\left(-\tfrac{3}{2}+4\chi\right)T_{k}
+α⁡[Ca​(12+4​χ)+2​C​Nbρ]​β2\displaystyle+\alpha\left[{C_{\rm a}}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}+4\chi\right)+\frac{2CN_{\rm b}}{\rho}\right]\beta^{2}

We construct (A,u)(A,u) in Sections B.1–B.2 and prove the comparison-oracle bound in Sections B.3–B.4. Lemma B.16 then gives the ordinary first-order benchmark. B.1.2 A smooth decomposition for the gradient oracle

The decomposition CT=BT−WTC_{T}=B_{T}-W_{T} separates the part of the gradient that may expose the next coordinate. We define its deterministic weights below; randomness enters through (77).

Fix once and for all a nondecreasing function Γ∈C∞​(ℝ,[0,1])\Gamma\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R};[0,1]) such that

Γ⁡(t)=0(t≤1/4),Γ⁡(t)=1(t≥1/2).\Gamma(t)=0\quad(t\leq 1/4),\qquad\Gamma(t)=1\quad(t\geq 1/2). (72)

Set

This is smooth because it vanishes on a neighborhood of the origin. For i∈[T]i\in[T], define

ri​(v):=(∑j=iTγ​(vj)2)1/2,Θi​(v):=Γ⁡(1−ri​(v)).r_{i}(v):=\left(\sum_{j=i}^{T}\gamma(v_{j})^{2}\right)^{1/2},\qquad\Theta_{i}(v):=\Gamma(1-r_{i}(v)). (73)

B.3 Finite-channel random rotation

The comparison oracle returns two ambient vectors and a scalar. We prove a random-rotation bound that permits these separate channels, including the scalar information, and applies to arbitrary adaptive queries and final outputs.

Definition B.7 (Uniform finite-channel probability-ϖ\varpi zero-chain).

Fix ϖ∈[0,1]\varpi\in[0,1]. Let 𝒴,Ξ,𝒮\mathcal{Y},\Xi,\mathcal{S} be standard Borel spaces, let ξ∼ν\xi\sim\nu, and let

s:ℝT×𝒴×Ξ→𝒮,s:\mathbb{R}^{T}\times\mathcal{Y}\times\Xi\to\mathcal{S},

be Borel maps. We call (s,a(1),…,a(m))(s,a^{(1)},\ldots,a^{(m)}) a uniform finite-channel probability-ϖ\varpi zero-chain if there is a measurable event E⊆ΞE\subseteq\Xi with ν⁡(E)≤ϖ\nu(E)\leq\varpi such that, for every (v,y,ξ)(v,y,\xi),

maxℓ∈[m]⁡prog0⁡(a(ℓ)​(v,y,ξ))≤prog1/4⁡(v)+1,\max_{\ell\in[m]}\operatorname{prog}_{0}(a^{(\ell)}(v,y,\xi))\leq\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}(v)+1, (119)

Lemma B.9 (Invariant posterior under an invariant observation).

Let 𝖢,𝖷,𝖹\mathsf{C},\mathsf{X},\mathsf{Z} be standard Borel spaces, let GG be a compact second-countable group with normalized Haar probability λG\lambda_{G}, and let

τ:𝖢×G×𝖷→𝖷\tau:\mathsf{C}\times G\times\mathsf{X}\to\mathsf{X}

be a Borel map such that g↦τc,gg\mapsto\tau_{c,g} is a group action for every cc. Let K⁡(c,d​x)K(c,dx) be a Borel probability kernel satisfying

K⁡(c,τc,g−1​A)=K⁡(c,A)(c∈𝖢,g∈G)K(c,\tau_{c,g}^{-1}A)=K(c,A)\qquad(c\in\mathsf{C},\ g\in G) (128)

for every Borel A⊆𝖷A\subseteq\mathsf{X}. Suppose that the Borel observation H:𝖢×𝖷→𝖹H:\mathsf{C}\times\mathsf{X}\to\mathsf{Z} is invariant:

H⁡(c,τc,g​x)=H⁡(c,x).H(c,\tau_{c,g}x)=H(c,x). (129)

Then there is a Borel regular conditional kernel L⁡(c,v,d​x)L(c,v,dx) for xx given v=H⁡(c,x)v=H(c,x) under K⁡(c,d​x)K(c,dx) such that

L⁡(c,v,τc,g−1​A)=L⁡(c,v,A)L(c,v,\tau_{c,g}^{-1}A)=L(c,v,A) (130)

for every g∈Gg\in G and for H​(c,⋅)#​K​(c)H(c,\cdot)_{\#}K(c)-almost every vv.

Proof.

Let L0​(c,v,d​x)L_{0}(c,v,dx) be any Borel disintegration of K⁡(c,d​x)K(c,dx) over the map H⁡(c,⋅)H(c,\cdot), and define

L⁡(c,v,A):=∫GL0​(c,v,τc,g−1​A)​λG​(𝑑g).L(c,v,A):=\int_{G}L_{0}(c,v,\tau_{c,g}^{-1}A)\,\lambda_{G}(dg). (131)

This is a Borel kernel. If M⁡(c,d​v):=H​(c,⋅)#​K​(c)M(c,dv):=H(c,\cdot)_{\#}K(c), then for Borel A⊆𝖷A\subseteq\mathsf{X} and B⊆𝖹B\subseteq\mathsf{Z},

∫BL⁡(c,v,A)​M​(c,𝑑v)\displaystyle\int_{B}L(c,v,A)M(c,dv) =∫GK⁡(c,τc,g−1​A∩H​(c,⋅)−1​B)​λG​(𝑑g)\displaystyle=\int_{G}K\bigl(c,\tau_{c,g}^{-1}A\cap H(c,\cdot)^{-1}B\bigr)\,\lambda_{G}(dg)
=∫GK⁡(c,τc,g−1​(A∩H​(c,⋅)−1​B))​λG​(𝑑g)\displaystyle=\int_{G}K\bigl(c,\tau_{c,g}^{-1}(A\cap H(c,\cdot)^{-1}B)\bigr)\,\lambda_{G}(dg)
=K⁡(c,A∩H​(c,⋅)−1​B),\displaystyle=K\bigl(c,A\cap H(c,\cdot)^{-1}B\bigr),

where the second line uses (129) and the third uses (128). Hence LL is a regular conditional kernel. Equation (130) follows directly from (131) and left/right invariance of Haar probability on the compact group GG. ∎

Lemma B.10 (Sequential posterior-stabilizer invariance).

Let U=[u1,…,uT]U=[u_{1},\ldots,u_{T}] have the uniform invariant Stiefel distribution on Ortho⁡(d,T)\operatorname{Ortho}(d,T), and let ϑ\vartheta be an independent random element of a standard Borel space. Fix j∈[T]j\in[T] and an integer r≥0r\geq 0. Suppose that Borel maps χq\chi_{q} define recursively

xq=χq​(ϑ,u1,…,uj−1,v1,…,vq−1),vq=U⊤​xq,q∈[r].x_{q}=\chi_{q}(\vartheta,u_{1},\ldots,u_{j-1},v_{1},\ldots,v_{q-1}),\qquad v_{q}=U^{\top}x_{q},\qquad q\in[r]. (132)

Let

Cq:=(ϑ,u1,…,uj−1,v1,…,vq),C_{q}:=(\vartheta,u_{1},\ldots,u_{j-1},v_{1},\ldots,v_{q}),

with C0=(ϑ,u1,…,uj−1)C_{0}=(\vartheta,u_{1},\ldots,u_{j-1}), and set

𝖲q:=span⁡{u1,…,uj−1,x1,…,xq}.\mathsf{S}_{q}:=\operatorname{span}\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{j-1},x_{1},\ldots,x_{q}\}.

Regular conditional kernels Kq​(Cq,d​U)K_{q}(C_{q},dU) of UU given CqC_{q} may be chosen so that, for almost every Cq=cqC_{q}=c_{q}, the kernel is invariant under every orthogonal map fixing 𝖲q​(cq)\mathsf{S}_{q}(c_{q}) pointwise:

Kq​(cq,W−1​A)=Kq​(cq,A)whenever ​W​s=s​ for all ​s∈𝖲q​(cq).K_{q}(c_{q},W^{-1}A)=K_{q}(c_{q},A)\quad\text{whenever }Ws=s\text{ for all }s\in\mathsf{S}_{q}(c_{q}). (133)
Proof.

We construct the kernels inductively. Conditional on u1,…,uj−1u_{1},\ldots,u_{j-1}, the remaining columns of a uniform Stiefel frame have the standard invariant-completion law. Explicitly, after choosing a Borel orthonormal frame Q⟂​(u<j)Q_{\perp}(u_{<j}) for span⁡(u1,…,uj−1)⟂\operatorname{span}(u_{1},\ldots,u_{j-1})^{\perp}, this law is the image of the uniform invariant probability measure on the Stiefel manifold Ortho⁡(d−j+1,T−j+1)\operatorname{Ortho}(d-j+1,T-j+1) under

V⟼[u1,…,uj−1,Q⟂​(u<j)​V].V\longmapsto[u_{1},\ldots,u_{j-1},Q_{\perp}(u_{<j})V].

It is invariant under every orthogonal map fixing 𝖲0=span⁡{u1,…,uj−1}\mathsf{S}_{0}=\operatorname{span}\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{j-1}\} pointwise. Independence of ϑ\vartheta gives the required kernel K0K_{0}.

Assume that Kq−1K_{q-1} has been chosen. Let 𝖢q−1good\mathsf{C}_{q-1}^{\rm good} be a Borel full-measure subset of the conditioning space on which the induction hypothesis holds. We first restrict the conditioning parameter and the kernel to this good set; only after constructing the next posterior there will we extend it arbitrarily over the null complement. Once Cq−1=cq−1∈𝖢q−1goodC_{q-1}=c_{q-1}\in\mathsf{C}_{q-1}^{\rm good} is fixed, the vector xqx_{q} in (132) is fixed. Put

𝖲q=span⁡(𝖲q−1,xq).\mathsf{S}_{q}=\operatorname{span}(\mathsf{S}_{q-1},x_{q}).

On each stratum on which dim𝖲q=s\dim\mathsf{S}_{q}=s, choose a Borel orthogonal completion Q⟂​(cq−1)Q_{\perp}(c_{q-1}) of 𝖲q\mathsf{S}_{q}. For R∈O⁡(d−s)R\in O(d-s) define

Wcq−1,R:=P𝖲q+Q⟂​(cq−1)​R​Q⟂​(cq−1)⊤.W_{c_{q-1},R}:=P_{\mathsf{S}_{q}}+Q_{\perp}(c_{q-1})RQ_{\perp}(c_{q-1})^{\top}.

This is a Borel action of the fixed compact group O⁡(d−s)O(d-s) on the conditional Stiefel fiber. Because it fixes 𝖲q\mathsf{S}_{q} pointwise, it belongs to the stabilizer from the induction hypothesis. Moreover, the new observation

Hq​(cq−1,U):=U⊤​xqH_{q}(c_{q-1},U):=U^{\top}x_{q}

is invariant under this action:

(Wcq−1,R​U)⊤​xq=U⊤​Wcq−1,R⊤​xq=U⊤​xq.(W_{c_{q-1},R}U)^{\top}x_{q}=U^{\top}W_{c_{q-1},R}^{\top}x_{q}=U^{\top}x_{q}.

Apply Lemma B.9, separately on each Borel rank stratum of 𝖢q−1good\mathsf{C}_{q-1}^{\rm good}, to disintegrate Kq−1K_{q-1} over HqH_{q}. The finitely many resulting kernels paste into a Borel kernel on the good set; extend that kernel arbitrarily over the null complement. The resulting KqK_{q} is a regular conditional law given CqC_{q} and, for almost every CqC_{q}, is invariant under the full pointwise stabilizer of 𝖲q\mathsf{S}_{q}. This closes the induction. Every orthogonal transformation used in this argument is fixed only after Cq−1C_{q-1} has been conditioned upon; no state-dependent global change of variables is invoked. ∎

Lemma B.11 (Conditional residual spherical law; cf. Lemma 14 of Arjevani et al. (2023)).

Fix i∈[n]i\in[n] and j∈[T]j\in[T]. On the event 𝒯j(i−1)\mathcal{T}_{j}^{(i-1)}, the past transcript and the current query (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}) are measurable from 𝒰j−1(i−1)\mathcal{U}_{j-1}^{(i-1)}. In particular, 𝒯j(i−1)\mathcal{T}_{j}^{(i-1)}, the space

𝖲:=span⁡{u1,…,uj−1,x1,…,xi−1},\mathsf{S}:=\operatorname{span}\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{j-1},x_{1},\ldots,x_{i-1}\},

and its orthogonal projector are measurable under this conditioning. There is an 𝒰j−1(i−1)\mathcal{U}_{j-1}^{(i-1)}-measurable radius ri,j∈[0,1]r_{i,j}\in[0,1] such that, outside a null event and on 𝒯j(i−1)\mathcal{T}_{j}^{(i-1)},

ℒ(P𝖲⟂uj|𝒰j−1(i−1))={δ0,ri,j=0,Unif⁡({v∈𝖲⟂:‖v‖=ri,j}),ri,j>0.\mathcal{L}\!\left(P_{\mathsf{S}^{\perp}}u_{j}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{U}_{j-1}^{(i-1)}\right)=\begin{cases}\delta_{0},&r_{i,j}=0,\\[2.84526pt] \operatorname{Unif}\!\left(\{v\in\mathsf{S}^{\perp}:\left\lVert v\right\rVert=r_{i,j}\}\right),&r_{i,j}>0.\end{cases} (134)

Moreover, ri,j=‖P𝖲⟂​uj‖r_{i,j}=\left\lVert P_{\mathsf{S}^{\perp}}u_{j}\right\rVert almost surely. Thus normalization is used only on {ri,j>0}\{r_{i,j}>0\}.

Proof.

We first construct globally Borel quiet-simulated queries. For fixed u<j:=(u1,…,uj−1)u_{<j}:=(u_{1},\ldots,u_{j-1}), define the truncated canonical response

𝒪¯<j​(v,y,ξ,u<j):=(CLOSE\displaystyle\overline{\mathcal{O}}_{<j}(v,y;\xi,u_{<j}):=\biggl( OPENs⁡(v,y,ξ),∑r<j[a(1)​(v,y,ξ)]r​ur,…,∑r<j[a(m)​(v,y,ξ)]r​ur).\displaystyle s(v,y,\xi),\sum_{r<j}[a^{(1)}(v,y,\xi)]_{r}u_{r},\ldots,\sum_{r<j}[a^{(m)}(v,y,\xi)]_{r}u_{r}\biggr). (135)

Feed these responses recursively to the algorithm. Since all algorithm and oracle maps are Borel, there are Borel maps χq\chi_{q} such that, for ϑ:=(ξ0,ξ1,…,ξi−1)\vartheta:=(\xi_{0},\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{i-1}),

(x¯q,y¯q)=χq​(ϑ,u<j,v¯1,…,v¯q−1),v¯q:=U⊤​x¯q,q≤i.(\bar{x}_{q},\bar{y}_{q})=\chi_{q}(\vartheta,u_{<j},\bar{v}_{1},\ldots,\bar{v}_{q-1}),\qquad\bar{v}_{q}:=U^{\top}\bar{x}_{q},\qquad q\leq i. (136)

For q<iq<i, let γ¯q\bar{\gamma}_{q} be the progress computed from the corresponding latent coefficients a(ℓ)​(v¯q,y¯q,ξq)a^{(\ell)}(\bar{v}_{q},\bar{y}_{q},\xi_{q}).

A first-disagreement induction gives

{j>γi−1}={j>γ¯i−1},(xq,yq,vq)=(x¯q,y¯q,v¯q)(q≤i)\{j>\gamma_{i-1}\}=\{j>\bar{\gamma}_{i-1}\},\qquad(x_{q},y_{q},v_{q})=(\bar{x}_{q},\bar{y}_{q},\bar{v}_{q})\quad(q\leq i) (137)

on this common event. For the first implication, suppose j>γi−1j>\gamma_{i-1}. Then every actual latent coefficient before time ii is supported in {1,…,j−1}\{1,\ldots,j-1\}. Starting from the common first query, the actual ambient response therefore equals (135); induction gives equality of the two trajectories and hence γ¯i−1=γi−1<j\bar{\gamma}_{i-1}=\gamma_{i-1}<j. The reverse implication is identical with the roles of the actual and quiet trajectories interchanged.

For completeness, measurability from the actual conditioning tuple can be checked without referring to the random quiet trajectory. Given (ξ0,u<j,v1,ξ1,…,vi−1,ξi−1)(\xi_{0},u_{<j},v_{1},\xi_{1},\ldots,v_{i-1},\xi_{i-1}), recursively compute the query, the non-ambient channel, and the latent coefficients at each past round. If a coefficient first has support reaching jj, declare 𝒯j(i−1)\mathcal{T}_{j}^{(i-1)} false; while all coefficients remain supported below jj, every ambient response is computable from u<ju_{<j} and the recursion continues. The declaration is correct by induction and, on the true event, also reconstructs (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}). Hence 𝒯j(i−1)\mathcal{T}_{j}^{(i-1)} and the current query are 𝒰j−1(i−1)\mathcal{U}_{j-1}^{(i-1)}-measurable.

Apply Lemma B.10 to the quiet recursion (136), with r=i−1r=i-1. It yields a regular conditional kernel of UU given

(ϑ,u1,…,uj−1,v¯1,…,v¯i−1).(\vartheta,u_{1},\ldots,u_{j-1},\bar{v}_{1},\ldots,\bar{v}_{i-1}).

Transport this kernel through the fixed Borel coordinate reordering and write the conditioning tuple, in exactly the order used in (126), as

C¯:=(ξ0,u1,…,uj−1,v¯1,ξ1,…,v¯i−1,ξi−1).\bar{C}:=(\xi_{0},u_{1},\ldots,u_{j-1},\bar{v}_{1},\xi_{1},\ldots,\bar{v}_{i-1},\xi_{i-1}).

Denote the transported kernel by K¯​(C¯,d​U)\bar{K}(\bar{C},dU). It is invariant under every orthogonal map fixing

𝖲¯:=span⁡{u1,…,uj−1,x¯1,…,x¯i−1}\bar{\mathsf{S}}:=\operatorname{span}\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{j-1},\bar{x}_{1},\ldots,\bar{x}_{i-1}\}

pointwise. Let

C:=(ξ0,u1,…,uj−1,v1,ξ1,…,vi−1,ξi−1),C:=(\xi_{0},u_{1},\ldots,u_{j-1},v_{1},\xi_{1},\ldots,v_{i-1},\xi_{i-1}),

the tuple generating 𝒰j−1(i−1)\mathcal{U}_{j-1}^{(i-1)}. By (137), on 𝒯j(i−1)\mathcal{T}_{j}^{(i-1)} we now have the literal equality C¯=C\bar{C}=C, and 𝖲¯=𝖲\bar{\mathsf{S}}=\mathsf{S}. Write K¯​ϕ​(c):=∫ϕ⁡(U)​K¯​(c,𝑑U)\bar{K}\phi(c):=\int\phi(U)\bar{K}(c,dU). Because the events and the conditioning tuples agree in (137), for every bounded Borel hh and ϕ\phi,

𝔼⁡[𝟏𝒯j(i−1)​h​(C)​ϕ​(U)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{T}_{j}^{(i-1)}}h(C)\phi(U)\right] =𝔼[𝟏{j>γ¯i−1}h(C¯)ϕ(U)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbf{1}_{\{j>\bar{\gamma}_{i-1}\}}h(\bar{C})\phi(U)\right]
=𝔼[𝟏{j>γ¯i−1}h(C¯)K¯ϕ(C¯)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbf{1}_{\{j>\bar{\gamma}_{i-1}\}}h(\bar{C})\bar{K}\phi(\bar{C})\right]
=𝔼⁡[𝟏𝒯j(i−1)​h​(C)​K¯​ϕ​(C)].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{T}_{j}^{(i-1)}}h(C)\bar{K}\phi(C)\right].

Thus K¯​(C,⋅)\bar{K}(C,\cdot) is a version of the actual conditional law on 𝒯j(i−1)\mathcal{T}_{j}^{(i-1)}. We have therefore obtained, by a sequential posterior-kernel induction, the conditional invariance of UU under the pointwise stabilizer of 𝖲\mathsf{S}. In particular, the conditional law of uju_{j} is invariant under that stabilizer.

It remains to identify its orbit. The conditioning fixes all inner products of uju_{j} with the spanning vectors of 𝖲\mathsf{S}: they are zero against u1,…,uj−1u_{1},\ldots,u_{j-1}, and

⟨uj,xq⟩=[vq]j,q<i.\left\langle u_{j},x_{q}\right\rangle=[v_{q}]_{j},\qquad q<i.

These values determine b:=P𝖲​ujb:=P_{\mathsf{S}}u_{j} uniquely, even when the spanning vectors are linearly dependent. Since ‖uj‖=1\left\lVert u_{j}\right\rVert=1, they also determine the Borel radius

ri,j:=1−‖b‖2=‖P𝖲⟂​uj‖.r_{i,j}:=\sqrt{1-\left\lVert b\right\rVert^{2}}=\left\lVert P_{\mathsf{S}^{\perp}}u_{j}\right\rVert.

The residual conditional law is supported on the radius-ri,jr_{i,j} sphere in 𝖲⟂\mathsf{S}^{\perp} and is invariant under its full orthogonal group. For ri,j>0r_{i,j}>0, uniqueness of rotation-invariant spherical probability gives the second case of (134); for ri,j=0r_{i,j}=0, the sphere is the singleton {0}\{0\} and the law is δ0\delta_{0}. ∎

Lemma B.12 (One-pair guessing estimate; cf. Lemma 13 of Arjevani et al. (2023)).

Use the projections and events 𝒢j(i)\mathcal{G}_{j}^{(i)} from Lemma B.8, with the random query sequence x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n}. If d>n+Td>n+T, then, for every i∈[n]i\in[n] and j∈[T]j\in[T],

ℙ⁡((𝒢j(i))c,𝒯j(i−1))≤2​exp⁡(−d−i−j32​R2​n)≤2​exp⁡(−d−n−T32​R2​n).\mathbb{P}\left((\mathcal{G}_{j}^{(i)})^{c},\mathcal{T}_{j}^{(i-1)}\right)\leq 2\exp\!\left(-\frac{d-i-j}{32R^{2}n}\right)\leq 2\exp\!\left(-\frac{d-n-T}{32R^{2}n}\right). (138)
Proof.

Work on 𝒯j(i−1)\mathcal{T}_{j}^{(i-1)} and condition on 𝒰j−1(i−1)\mathcal{U}_{j-1}^{(i-1)}. Put

𝖲=span⁡{u1,…,uj−1,x1,…,xi−1},P=P𝖲⟂=Pj−1(i−1),\mathsf{S}=\operatorname{span}\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{j-1},x_{1},\ldots,x_{i-1}\},\qquad P=P_{\mathsf{S}^{\perp}}=P_{j-1}^{(i-1)},

Πj−1(i)​Pj−1(i−1)​uj=0;\Pi_{j-1}^{(i)}P_{j-1}^{(i-1)}u_{j}=0;

the conditional probability of the bad event is therefore zero.

Suppose now that r>0r>0 and define u^j:=P​uj/r\widehat{u}_{j}:=Pu_{j}/r. By Lemma B.11, u^j\widehat{u}_{j} is uniform on the unit sphere of 𝖲⟂\mathsf{S}^{\perp}. Since r≤1r\leq 1,

ℙ⁡(‖Πj−1(i)​Pj−1(i−1)​uj‖≥14​R​n|𝒰j−1(i−1))\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\left\lVert\Pi_{j-1}^{(i)}P_{j-1}^{(i-1)}u_{j}\right\rVert\geq\frac{1}{4R\sqrt{n}}\ \middle|\ \mathcal{U}_{j-1}^{(i-1)}\right)
≤ℙ⁡(‖Πj−1(i)​u^j‖≥14​R​n|𝒰j−1(i−1)).\displaystyle\qquad\leq\mathbb{P}\left(\left\lVert\Pi_{j-1}^{(i)}\widehat{u}_{j}\right\rVert\geq\frac{1}{4R\sqrt{n}}\ \middle|\ \mathcal{U}_{j-1}^{(i-1)}\right).
